A uniform magnetic field $\vec{B}$ is perpendicular to the plane of the paper and extends from $x=0$ to $x=b$ and it is zero from $x>b$ . The magnitude of emf Induced in the conductor is
questions.question_html: In the figure shown, the conductor PQ of length $l$ is moved from $x=0$ to $x=b$ and then up to $x=2b$ with a constant velocity $\vec{v}$ . A uniform magnetic field $\vec{B}$ is perpendicular to the plane of the paper and extends from $x=0$ to $x=b$ and it is zero from $x>b$ . The magnitude of emf Induced in the conductor is

options.label: A
options.html: $Blx;0 \le x \le b$

options.label: B
options.html: Zero; $0 \le x \le b$

options.label: C
options.html: $Blv;0 \le x \le b$

questions.explanation_text: When conductor PQ moves from $x=0$ to $x=b$ , it is inside the uniform magnetic field $\vec{B}$ . The magnetic field is perpendicular to the plane of the paper. The conductor has length $l$ and moves with constant velocity $\vec{v}$ . For a straight conductor moving perpendicular to a magnetic field, the motional emf induced across its ends is $E=Blv$ Here, $B$ , $l$ , and $v$ are constant. So, the induced emf remains constant while the conductor is in the region $0 \le x \le b$ . When the conductor moves from $x=b$ to $x=2b$ , it is outside the magnetic field region. In this region, the magnetic field is zero, so $B=0$ . Hence, the induced emf is also zero from $x=b$ to $x=2b$ . Thus, the magnitude of emf induced is $Blv$ for $0 \le x \le b$ .
questions.explanation_html:
When conductor PQ moves from $x=0$ to $x=b$ , it is inside the uniform magnetic field $\vec{B}$ .

The magnetic field is perpendicular to the plane of the paper. The conductor has length $l$ and moves with constant velocity $\vec{v}$ .

For a straight conductor moving perpendicular to a magnetic field, the motional emf induced across its ends is

$E=Blv$

Here, $B$ , $l$ , and $v$ are constant. So, the induced emf remains constant while the conductor is in the region $0 \le x \le b$ .

When the conductor moves from $x=b$ to $x=2b$ , it is outside the magnetic field region.

In this region, the magnetic field is zero, so $B=0$ .

Hence, the induced emf is also zero from $x=b$ to $x=2b$ .

Thus, the magnitude of emf induced is $Blv$ for $0 \le x \le b$ .

The pointer in the galvanometer deflects - (a) When the bar magnet is moved towards the stationary coil along its axis. (b) When the bar magnet is moved away from the stationary coil along its axis. (c) When the coil is moved towards the stationary bar magnet along its axis. (d) When the coil and the magnet are moved without relative motion between them.
questions.question_html:
In Faraday-Henry's experiment, a coil is connected to a galvanometer. For the deflection of pointer in the galvanometer, which of the following statement/s is/are WRONG?
The pointer in the galvanometer deflects -
(a) When the bar magnet is moved towards the stationary coil along its axis.
(b) When the bar magnet is moved away from the stationary coil along its axis.
(c) When the coil is moved towards the stationary bar magnet along its axis.
(d) When the coil and the magnet are moved without relative motion between them.

options.label: A
options.html: a and b

options.label: B
options.html: b and c

options.label: C
options.html: a, b and c

questions.explanation_text: The wrong statement is (d) . In Faraday-Henry’s experiment, the galvanometer pointer deflects only when the magnetic flux linked with the coil changes. When there is relative motion between the magnet and the coil, the magnetic flux through the coil changes. So an induced current is produced, and the galvanometer shows deflection. Now check each case: (a) When the bar magnet is moved towards the stationary coil, the magnetic flux through the coil changes. So the pointer deflects. This statement is correct. (b) When the bar magnet is moved away from the stationary coil, the magnetic flux again changes, but in the opposite way. So the pointer deflects in the opposite direction. This statement is also correct. (c) When the coil is moved towards the stationary bar magnet, there is still relative motion between the coil and magnet. So the flux changes and the pointer deflects. This statement is correct. (d) When the coil and the magnet are moved together without relative motion, the magnetic flux linked with the coil does not change. So no induced current is produced, and the galvanometer pointer does not deflect. Hence, the wrong statement is: $\text{Only d}$ Correct option: Option D .
questions.explanation_html:
The wrong statement is (d).

In Faraday-Henry’s experiment, the galvanometer pointer deflects only when the magnetic flux linked with the coil changes.

When there is relative motion between the magnet and the coil, the magnetic flux through the coil changes. So an induced current is produced, and the galvanometer shows deflection.

Now check each case:

(a) When the bar magnet is moved towards the stationary coil, the magnetic flux through the coil changes.

So the pointer deflects. This statement is correct.

(b) When the bar magnet is moved away from the stationary coil, the magnetic flux again changes, but in the opposite way.

So the pointer deflects in the opposite direction. This statement is also correct.

(c) When the coil is moved towards the stationary bar magnet, there is still relative motion between the coil and magnet.

So the flux changes and the pointer deflects. This statement is correct.

(d) When the coil and the magnet are moved together without relative motion, the magnetic flux linked with the coil does not change.

So no induced current is produced, and the galvanometer pointer does not deflect.

Hence, the wrong statement is:

$\text{Only d}$

Correct option: Option D.

questions.explanation_text: According to Lenz's Law, a changing magnetic flux through a coil induces an electromotive force (EMF) that opposes the change in flux. When a bar magnet is pushed towards the coil, the change in magnetic flux through the coil causes the galvanometer pointer to deflect in one direction (towards X, in this case). Conversely, when the bar magnet is pulled away from the coil, the change in magnetic flux is in the opposite direction. Thus, the galvanometer pointer will deflect in the opposite direction, which is towards $X^{1}$ . This occurs as the system attempts to oppose the change in magnetic flux by inducing a current that produces a magnetic field opposing the original direction.

$\therefore$ No emf is induced.

questions.question_html: The magnetic flux linked with a coil varies as $\phi=3t^{2}+4t+9$ . The magnitude of the emf induced at $t=2s$ is
questions.explanation_text: To find the induced emf, we use Faraday's law of electromagnetic induction, which states that the induced emf (𝜀) in a coil is given by: $\epsilon=-\frac{d\phi}{dt}$ Here, the flux is given by: $\phi(t)=3t^{2}+4t+9$ Step-by-step calculation: Differentiate the flux with respect to time: $\frac{d\phi}{dt}=\frac{d}{dt}(3t^{2}+4t+9)=6t+4$ Substitute $t=2$ seconds: $\frac{d\phi}{dt}|_{t=2}=6(2)+4=12+4=16$ The induced emf is the negative of this derivative, but we are asked for the magnitude. Therefore: $|\epsilon|=|-16|=16\text{V}$ So, the magnitude of the induced emf at $t=2\text{s}$ is 16 V. Answer: Option C 16 V.
questions.explanation_html:
To find the induced emf, we use Faraday's law of electromagnetic induction, which states that the induced emf (𝜀) in a coil is given by:

$\epsilon=-\frac{d\phi}{dt}$

Here, the flux is given by:

$\phi(t)=3t^{2}+4t+9$

Step-by-step calculation:

Differentiate the flux with respect to time:

$\frac{d\phi}{dt}=\frac{d}{dt}(3t^{2}+4t+9)=6t+4$

Substitute $t=2$ seconds:

$\frac{d\phi}{dt}|_{t=2}=6(2)+4=12+4=16$

The induced emf is the negative of this derivative, but we are asked for the magnitude. Therefore:

$|\epsilon|=|-16|=16\text{V}$

So, the magnitude of the induced emf at $t=2\text{s}$ is 16 V.

Answer: Option C 16 V.

questions.question_html: A step-up transformer operates on a 230 V "ne and a load current of 2 A . The ratio of primary and secondary windings is $1:25$ . Then, the current in the primary is
questions.explanation_text: Let's break down the solution step by step: Since the transformer is a step-up type with a ratio of primary to secondary windings of $1:25$ , the secondary voltage is: $V_{s}=25 \times 230\text{V}=5750\text{V}$ Assuming the transformer is ideal (no energy losses), the input power equals the output power: $V_{p}I_{p}=V_{s}I_{s}$ Rearranging to solve for the primary current $I_{p}$ : $I_{p}=\frac{V_{s}I_{s}}{V_{p}}$ Substitute the known values: $I_{p}=\frac{5750\text{V} \times 2\text{A}}{230\text{V}}=\frac{11500}{230}=50\text{A}$ Therefore, the current in the primary is $50\text{A}$ , which corresponds to Option B.
questions.explanation_html:
Let's break down the solution step by step:

Since the transformer is a step-up type with a ratio of primary to secondary windings of $1:25$ , the secondary voltage is:

$V_{s}=25 \times 230\text{V}=5750\text{V}$

Assuming the transformer is ideal (no energy losses), the input power equals the output power:

$V_{p}I_{p}=V_{s}I_{s}$

Rearranging to solve for the primary current $I_{p}$ :

$I_{p}=\frac{V_{s}I_{s}}{V_{p}}$

Substitute the known values:

$I_{p}=\frac{5750\text{V} \times 2\text{A}}{230\text{V}}=\frac{11500}{230}=50\text{A}$

Therefore, the current in the primary is $50\text{A}$ , which corresponds to Option B.

questions.question_html: A jet plane of wing span 20 m is travelling towards west at a speed of $400ms^{-1}$ . If the earth's total magnetic field is $4 \times 10^{-4}T$ and the dip angle is $30^{\circ}$ , at that place, then the voltage differences developed across the ends of the wing is
questions.explanation_text: Given: Speed $v=400m/s$ Magnetic field $B=4 \times 10^{-4}T$ Dip angle $\theta=30^{\circ}$ To find the voltage difference developed across the ends of the wing, we use the formula: $\text{Voltage difference}=B \cdot l \cdot v \cdot sin\theta$ Substituting the given values: $\begin{aligned} \text{Voltage difference} & =4 \times 10^{-4} \cdot 20 \cdot 400 \cdot sin30^{\circ} \\ & =32000 \times 10^{-4} \times sin30^{\circ} \\ & =32000 \times 10^{-4} \cdot \frac{1}{2} \\ & =1.6V \end{aligned}$ Thus, the voltage difference across the ends of the wing is $1.6V$ .
questions.explanation_html:
Given:

Speed $v=400m/s$

Magnetic field $B=4 \times 10^{-4}T$

Dip angle $\theta=30^{\circ}$

To find the voltage difference developed across the ends of the wing, we use the formula:

$\text{Voltage difference}=B \cdot l \cdot v \cdot sin\theta$

Substituting the given values:

$\begin{aligned} \text{Voltage difference} & =4 \times 10^{-4} \cdot 20 \cdot 400 \cdot sin30^{\circ} \\ & =32000 \times 10^{-4} \times sin30^{\circ} \\ & =32000 \times 10^{-4} \cdot \frac{1}{2} \\ & =1.6V \end{aligned}$

Thus, the voltage difference across the ends of the wing is $1.6V$ .

questions.explanation_text: Magnetic braking in trains works on the principle of eddy currents. Here’s a quick breakdown: When a magnet moves relative to a conductive material (like aluminum), it induces circular currents (eddy currents) in that conductor. According to Lenz's law, these eddy currents create their own magnetic fields that oppose the motion causing them. This opposition produces a braking force, which helps in slowing down the train without physical friction. So, the correct answer is: $\text{Option A: eddy current.}$

So, the correct answer is:

$\text{Option A: eddy current.}$
